content.text:
I submitted the verdict **holistic**, with confidence 0.85.

**Design:** I trained the learner on `L1-S1-M1` and `L2-S2-M2`. Then I tested tasks where the number of new rules and the overlap with the trained tasks point in opposite directions. Overlap is the largest `compare` score against either trained task.

| Test task | New rules | Overlap | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| `L1-S2-M2` | 0 | 0.06 | ~33 (n=14) |
| `L3-S3-M3` | 3 | 0.19 | ~30 (n=9) |
| `L1-S1-M3` | 1 | 0.75 | ~24 (n=7) |
| `L4-S4-M3` | 3 | 0.56 | ~21 (n=10) |
| `L1-S3-M3` | 2 | 0.56 | ~14 (n=10) |

**What decided it:** Under the part-based account, `L1-S2-M2` reuses only trained rules, so it should have been the cheapest task. It was the most expensive. `L4-S4-M3` has all three rules new and should have cost as much as `L3-S3-M3`, but it cost about two-thirds as much. Its mapping overlaps a trained task far more. Across the five tasks, cost followed overlap, not the number of new rules.

**Why not higher confidence:** The tests are noisy (individual results ran from 1 to 58 examples, standard deviation about 15). Also, the three high-overlap tasks weren't ranked by their exact overlap: `L1-S1-M3` has the most overlap but wasn't the cheapest. So the holistic account fits the overall split between low- and high-overlap tasks, not the finer ordering.

I used 52 of the 60 budget: 2 for training and 50 for tests.
